title: Mind first
hookLine: spending too long on the body is a sign of neglecting the mind (Enchiridion 41)

cards: Add it up for one ordinary day. The workout. The shower and the hair.
The meals, the snacks, the planning of meals. The skincare, the mirror, the step count on the watch.
Now add up the minutes that went to the mind on purpose: thinking something through, reading something that stretched you, asking whether a judgment was true. Which list is longer?
Epictetus doesn't ask you to drop the first one. He asks you to look at the ratio.

teach.h: TOO MUCH TIME ON THE BODY.
teach.b: It's a sign of a dull nature, Epictetus says, to spend a lot of time on the things of the body: a lot of exercise, a lot of eating, a lot of drinking, and the rest of the body's business. The key words are a lot.
He isn't against the body. His own teacher, Musonius Rufus, taught that students should train the body as well as the soul, through cold and heat and hard work.
Epictetus doesn't forbid eating, drinking or exercise either. He asks you to notice when the body's business takes up the whole day.

teach.h: DO THE BODY'S THINGS IN PASSING.
teach.b: These things, he says, should be done in passing, along the way.

teach.h: GNŌMĒ: TURN YOUR CARE TO THE MIND.
teach.b: All your care should turn toward the mind. The Greek here is gnōmē, a word for judgment, outlook, the way a person thinks things through.
For the Stoics, that's where a life actually gets lived: in how you judge what happens. A well-tended body with a neglected mind is like a beautifully kept house where no one ever opens the windows.
Why it's urgent: the body will be looked after whether you plan it or not. Hunger reminds you. Tiredness reminds you.
Nothing in the day reminds you to think.
The mind only gets its turn if you give it one on purpose. Not because the body doesn't matter, but because the mind is the one that gets forgotten.

how: Some people practicing Stoicism keep the body's routines simple and set aside a few deliberate minutes each day for reading, reflection or journaling.

o: do the body's business in passing; give real care to the mind
think through every choice before you take any action
ignore the body entirely so the mind can grow stronger

p: too much time on the body
a sign of a dull nature

s: Epictetus says to neglect the body entirely
the key word is a lot. do the body's things in passing.
his teacher Musonius Rufus included training the body
cold, heat and hard work, alongside the soul.

games.q: you have a free half hour. you've already worked out and planned dinner. what does Enchiridion 41 point to?
o: give the time to the mind: read, or think something through.
games.why: the body's business in passing, he says, and all your care toward the mind.

practice: Let the body sit and breathe for a minute, and give the mind its turn with one question that deserves real thought: something you believe and have never checked, a decision you keep putting off, a line from this handbook that bothered you.
Turn it over slowly, the way you'd turn a stone in your hand. No need to answer it; just think on purpose.

wordCard.voice: Mind first. Enchiridion forty-one: do the body's business in passing, and turn your real care toward the mind. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: judgment, outlook, mind, where Enchiridion 41 says to turn all your care.

carryVoice: Your line: open the windows. The body reminds you; the mind waits to be asked. Day three hundred seventy-six, done.
